scenes.say: Delete one word, virtual, and every shape prints zero. By the end, you'll explain the four pillars of O O P, and show when virtual picks the function.

Today you will do three things. Explain the four pillars with one Shape example. Tell inheritance, and its types, from polymorphism. And show when virtual, pure virtual, and abstract classes change the call.
lines: Explain the four pillars with one example

scenes.title: What are the four pillars of OOP?
scenes.statement: Explain the four pillars of object oriented programming with one example, and prove it with code.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, a Circle of radius two, and a Square of side three. Areas: twelve point five seven, and nine. Name four pillars with this.

scenes.head: Four pillars, one Shape
scenes.say: Four pillars, one Shape. Encapsulation: Circle keeps its radius private, so nobody sets it to minus five. Abstraction: Shape promises an area, and says nothing about how. Inheritance: a Circle is a Shape. Polymorphism: one call to area, and each shape answers for itself.

scenes.head: Abstraction and encapsulation in code
scenes.say: In code. Shape says what every shape can do: an area. Equals zero means no body here. That is abstraction. Circle hides its radius as private, and the constructor guards it. That is encapsulation.
Your turn. We build a Circle with radius minus five. The constructor guards it. What does area print? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Inheritance and polymorphism
scenes.say: Zero. The guard made the radius zero. Now Square also derives from Shape, so each one is a Shape. Put all three in a Shape pointer array, and loop. Same call, p arrow area, and each object runs its own formula: circle, square, and the guarded circle.

scenes.title: Encapsulation or abstraction?
scenes.statement: Two words that sound alike. Give each one a one-line definition and a code example.

example.output: guard the inside vs simplify the outside

scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, a private balance, and a Storage with save. Both hide something. What is the difference?
Your turn. An Account keeps its balance private. Outside code tries to set the balance to minus a thousand. What happens? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Guard the inside, simplify the outside
scenes.say: A compile error. Account bundles the balance with deposit, which rejects bad amounts. That is encapsulation. On the right, backup only knows save. Where it goes, it never sees. That is abstraction, like push back on a vector.

panels.label: encapsulation
abstraction

scenes.head: Encapsulation vs abstraction
scenes.say: Goal? Protect data, versus reduce complexity. It hides? State, versus details. It answers? Who may touch this, versus what does this do. They work together.

scenes.title: What is inheritance, and what kinds?
scenes.statement: A Dog is an Animal. Show what a Dog inherits, name the types of inheritance, and explain the diamond.

example.output: Dog gets eat(); age is protected

scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, Dog derives from Animal. What does Dog get for free? What kinds of inheritance exist? And what goes wrong when two bases share a base?

scenes.head: A Dog is an Animal
scenes.say: Animal is the base class. Dog derives from it, so a Dog is an Animal. Dog gets eat for free, and adds its own bark. Age is protected: hidden from the outside, but visible to derived classes like Dog.

scenes.head: Types of inheritance, by structure
scenes.say: Single: one base, one derived. Multilevel: a chain, Shape to Polygon to Square. Multiple: two bases at once, which C plus plus allows. Hierarchical: many classes sharing one base. Mix them, and you get hybrid, with its famous problem, the diamond.

scenes.head: The diamond, fixed with virtual
scenes.say: A Copier is a Scanner and a Printer, and both are Devices. Marking the bases virtual makes them share one single Device. So c dot id just works, and prints seven.
Your turn. Remove the word virtual from both bases. Now what does c dot id do? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Without virtual: two Devices
scenes.say: A compile error: ambiguous. Without virtual, a Copier holds two separate Device parts, one through Scanner, one through Printer. The compiler can't tell which id you mean.

panels.label: no virtual

output.text: error: request for member ‘id’ is ambiguous

scenes.head: Types by access mode
scenes.say: Base private members always stay hidden. Public inheritance keeps public public: the normal is a. Protected makes both protected. Private makes both private: implemented in terms of. Defaults: struct public, class private.

scenes.title: Which function runs?
scenes.statement: A base pointer points at a derived object. Which version of the function runs, and when is that decided?
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, an Animal pointer holding a Dog. We call speak. Which version runs, and when is that decided? One keyword decides.

scenes.head: Runtime polymorphism: virtual
scenes.say: Animal declares speak as virtual. Dog and Cat each override it. The loop holds pointers to Animal, and calls speak. Each object runs its own version: woof, then meow. Add a Cow later, and the loop works unchanged.
Your turn. Back to shapes. Delete the word virtual from Shape's area. The loop still calls p arrow area on a Circle and a Square. What prints? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Without `virtual`, `p->area()` on a Circle(2) and Square(3) prints...

scenes.head: Without virtual: the pointer's type decides
scenes.say: Zero, zero. Without virtual, the compiler goes by the pointer's type. The pointer says Shape, so Shape's area runs, for both. That is early binding. With virtual, the object's real type decides, at runtime.

scenes.head: How a virtual call finds its function
scenes.say: Here pet points at a Dog object. Each object carries a hidden v pointer, which leads to the class's v table: an array of function pointers. The speak slot holds Dog speak. If the input said cat, the same call lands on Cat speak.

scenes.head: Trap one: virtual calls in a constructor
scenes.say: Two traps. First, a virtual call inside a constructor. While Base is being built, the Derived part doesn't exist yet. So the call goes to Base's version, not Derived's.

scenes.head: Trap two: the signature must match
scenes.say: Second, a signature mismatch. Run taking long does not override run taking int. Without override, that silently makes a new function. With override, the compiler refuses. So always write override.

output.text: error: ‘void Derived::run(long int)’ marked ‘override’, but does not override

scenes.title: Compile-time or runtime?
scenes.statement: Two ways to get one name, many behaviors. When is each decided, and what does each cost?

example.output: decided by the compiler vs by the object

scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, add with ints, and speak through an Animal pointer. One is settled before the program runs. The other, while it runs.

scenes.head: Compile time: overloads and templates
scenes.say: Overloading: the same name, different parameters. The compiler picks from the argument types. Templates: one piece of code, stamped out for each type you use. Both are settled before the program runs.

scenes.head: Compile time versus runtime
scenes.say: When? While compiling, versus while running. How? Overloads and templates, versus virtual functions through a base pointer. Call cost? Direct and inlinable, versus one indirect hop. Trade-off? Code bloat and slow builds, versus a small runtime overhead.
Your turn. A function takes an Animal by value, and we pass a Dog. It calls speak. Animal's speak prints three dots, Dog's prints woof. What prints? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `void f(Animal a) { a.speak(); }` called with a `Dog`. Prints...

scenes.head: The trap: slicing
scenes.say: Three dots. Passing by value copies only the Animal part, so the Dog is sliced away. By reference, the real type survives. Polymorphism needs virtual, override, and a pointer or reference.

scenes.title: Pure virtual and abstract
scenes.statement: Make a Shape that can't be created, yet forces every derived class to supply an area.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, area with equals zero. A plain Shape can't compute it, so creating one is an error.

scenes.head: Pure virtual makes a class abstract
scenes.say: Equals zero makes area pure virtual. A class with one is abstract: you can't create a Shape. Circle overrides area, so Circle is concrete. Shape pointers can still point at concrete objects.

scenes.head: An abstract class with real content
scenes.say: Abstract does not mean empty. Employee has a constructor, real data, and a normal function, printSlip. Only pay is missing, because the base can't know how an employee is paid. That is the template method pattern. A class of only pure virtuals is an interface.
Your turn. Polygon derives from Shape, adds a sides function, but never overrides area. We write Polygon p. What happens? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Polygon inherits pure `area()` and doesn't override it. `Polygon p;` is...

scenes.head: The obligation passes down
scenes.say: A compile error. Polygon still has the unimplemented area, so it is still abstract. The obligation passes down until some class overrides it.

output.text: error: cannot declare variable ‘p’ to be of abstract type ‘Polygon’

scenes.head: Surprise: a pure virtual can have a body
scenes.say: Interview surprise. A pure virtual function can still have a body, defined outside the class. Derived classes call it explicitly as a default. A pure virtual destructor must have a body, because every derived destructor calls it. Forget it, and you get a linker error.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Four pillars? Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism. Example? Shape: private radius, area, Circle is a Shape. Encapsulation versus abstraction? Guard the inside, simplify the outside.
rows: guard the inside, simplify the outside

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is inheritance? A derived class reuses a base, and public means is a. Types? Single, multilevel, multiple, hierarchical, hybrid. Diamond? Two copies of the base, fixed with virtual inheritance. Access modes? Public, protected, private.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is polymorphism? One interface, behavior chosen by the actual type. Compile time versus runtime? Overloads and templates, versus virtual functions. Cost? Direct call versus one vtable hop. Trap? Slicing: pass by reference or pointer.
rows: one interface, behavior by actual type
direct, inlinable vs one vtable hop

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is a virtual function? Chosen at runtime by the object's real type. How? A hidden vptr to the class's vtable. Traps? Constructor calls stay in Base, and always write override.
rows: chosen by the object's real type
ctor calls stay in Base; use `override`

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Pure virtual? Declared with equals zero. Abstract class? Has one, so can't be created. Can it have a body? Yes, and a pure virtual destructor must. Can an abstract class have data and a constructor? Yes, used through pointers.
rows: allowed; pure dtor must have one
yes; use via pointer or reference

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Try these three. LeetCode seven oh seven, design linked list, is private state behind a clean interface. LeetCode six forty one, design circular deque, hides a ring buffer. LeetCode one forty six, LRU cache, is an API over hidden structures.

So say this. Encapsulation guards the inside, abstraction simplifies the outside. Inheritance is an is a relationship, and virtual makes the object's real type choose the function. Pure virtual makes a class abstract.
lines: `virtual`: the real type picks the function.
Pure virtual = abstract: override to be concrete.
